prompts.research:
#data research
I am researching a federal dataset. Find out everything you can about this dataset, such as who publishes it, under what authority or mandate, its history, its typical users, and its benefits to the public. Be sure your research comprehensively covers each of those perspectives, as well as any others that you discover or seem useful. I believe this is accurate information, but please check:

Dataset title: Consumer Credit
Description: The G.19 Statistical Release, "Consumer Credit," reports outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, excluding loans secured by real estate. Total consumer credit comprises two major types: revolving and nonrevolving. The G.19 also reports selected terms of credit, including interest rates on new car loans, personal loans, and credit card plans at commercial banks. The G.19 also includes series that measure the terms of credit for new motor vehicle loans at finance companies.

Return a complete report on everything that a preservationist, data librarian, data scientist, or policy activist might want to know about this data.
prompts.assessment:
# Dataset risk assessment
I would like your help in assessing the likelihood that this data will be changed or removed from its primary location, and that users will no longer be able to access accurate and reliable copies of it, based on the rubric below.

## Sources for context
To help assess the rubric categories, perform additional research on the data, the agency, the data's topics and typical users, covering topics such as proposed regulatory or funding changes, recent news, and political commentary. Use whatever resources you find useful, including the Federal Register (https://www.federalregister.gov) and the federal staffing tracker at https://usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com.

## Rubric
This rubric is divided up into categories. Each category is divided up into risk levels. In your output, please select the appropriate risk level for each category based on your research.

### Historical Data Availability
- Gone: Data files prior to the current year or cycle are no longer publicly available.
- High Risk: Some data files prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- Moderate Risk: Some data elements that exist in the dataset prior to the current year or cycle are removed.
- No Known Issue: Data prior to the current year or cycle remain accessible with no known alterations.

### Future Data Availability
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Statutory publication deadline missed and/or collection or publication skipped and/or ICR expired for more than one year.
- Moderate Risk: Typical or intended publication date missed and/or collection or publication delayed; ICR expired up to one year.
- No Known Issue: Data published on time or as expected and ICR active or renewed before expiration.

### Data Quality
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Reductions in granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- Moderate Risk: Potential or emerging risk to granularity, timeliness, or frequency.
- No Known Issue: Maintained or improved granularity, timeliness, or frequency.

### Statutory Context
- Gone: N/A
- High Risk: Statutory authorization is vague and/or there are alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or no known programmatic use.
- Moderate Risk: Not explicitly required by statute but required for the implementation of a state or federal program, and there are no alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes.
- No Known Issue: Statutorily required and/or statutory authorization is explicitly named and it is clear what has to be collected, and there aren't alternative data collections that could serve as substitutes and/or required for implementation of a federal program.

### Staffing and Funding
- Gone: All of the staff in the division or agency are gone and/or all funding has been terminated.
- High Risk: 40% or more of staff lost, and/or 1,000 or more staff lost, and/or budget cut by 20% or more, and/or leadership removed.
- Moderate Risk: 10–39% of staff lost, and/or 500–999 staff lost, and/or budget cut by 10–19%, and/or threatened change in leadership.
- No Known Issue: Less than 10% of staff lost and less than 10% of budget cut and no known change in leadership.

### Policy
- Gone: Data collection and publication has been terminated.
- High Risk: Presidential Action-driven information collection request (ICR); negative policy note on site; other significant changes in accordance with Administration priorities.
- Moderate Risk: Proposed or pending changes; statements by administration officials suggesting a change is being considered or planned.
- No Known Issue: No notable changes since January 2025 affecting what data is collected and published.

For each category, concisely list the evidence and supporting sources that would support each risk level. Then indicate which risk level you find most appropriate and why.

Conclude with a simple summary of risk levels:
Historical Data Availability: <level>
Future Data Availability: <level>
Data Quality: <level>
Statutory Context: <level>
Staffing and Funding: <level>
Policy: <level>

## 1. Identification and Basic Facts

| Attribute | Detail |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Consumer Credit — G.19 Statistical Release |
| **Publisher** | Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System (Washington, D.C.) |
| **Frequency** | Monthly (released generally on the fifth business day of the month, covering the reference month roughly five weeks prior) |
| **Geography** | United States, national aggregates only |
| **Historical span** | Levels data back to January 1943 (seasonally adjusted total of ~$6.58 billion that month) |
| **Current magnitude** | Total consumer credit outstanding is on the order of $5 trillion |
| **Home page** | https://www.federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/ |
| **Division responsible** | Prepared by Board staff (Research and Statistics Division); released publicly by the Board's Public Affairs office |

**What it measures:** Outstanding credit extended to individuals for household, family, and other personal expenditures, *excluding loans secured by real estate* (mortgages and home equity products are covered instead in the Fed's Z.1 Financial Accounts). The two major components are:

- **Revolving credit** — open-ended plans up to a prearranged limit (mostly credit cards, plus items like prearranged overdraft plans)
- **Nonrevolving credit** — closed-end credit on a fixed repayment schedule (mostly motor vehicle and education loans, plus boat, RV, and personal loans)

The release also reports **selected terms of credit**: interest rates on new-car loans and personal loans and credit card plans at commercial banks, and terms (rates/maturities) of new motor vehicle loans at finance companies.

**Structure of the release:** Page 1 shows seasonally adjusted levels and annualized percent changes of total, revolving, and nonrevolving credit. Pages 2–3 show not-seasonally-adjusted levels and break-adjusted flows by **major holder**: depository institutions, finance companies, credit unions, the federal government, and nonprofit and educational institutions. Memo items track student loans and motor vehicle loans separately.

## 2. Publisher and Legal Authority / Mandate

**Who publishes it:** The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System — the federal agency that serves as the central bank of the United States and is the FOMC's home for monetary policy staff work.

**Legal and policy framework:**

- **Section 11 of the Federal Reserve Act** empowers the Board to require reports from depository institutions as necessary "to monitor and control monetary and credit aggregates" — the general statutory foundation for the Board's statistical programs.
- The Board's specific consumer-credit role dates to **Executive Order 8843 (August 9, 1941)**, issued by President Roosevelt under the national-emergency powers of the Trading with the Enemy Act framework (section 5(b) of the Act of October 6, 1917, as amended). The E.O. designated the Board as the agency to regulate consumer installment credit for defense mobilization — to curb inflation, divert resources to defense production, and prevent a postwar consumer-debt overhang. This produced **Regulation W**, which imposed down-payment and maximum-maturity limits on installment credit.
- The Board has been **the primary producer of aggregate consumer credit statistics since 1942**, "stemming from the Federal Reserve's responsibility for monetary policy and its particular responsibilities and data needs in the consumer credit area, originally under Executive Order 8843… and Board Regulation W… and later under various other acts and regulations" (the credit-control authority later resided in the Credit Control Act of 1969, which was briefly activated in 1980 and expired in 1982; Regulation W itself was terminated in 1952).
- **Terms-of-credit collection began in 1972** at the request of the President's Committee on Interest and Dividends, established as part of Phase I of President Nixon's wage-price controls program.
- The release operates within the framework of **OMB statistical policy**, including Statistical Policy Directive No. 3 (which sets release-timing goals for principal economic indicators). The Board acknowledges the G.19's ~5-week lag exceeds Directive No. 3's goal of release within 22 working days of the reference period, but states this is the shortest feasible lag given collection and review requirements. Periodic "Performance Evaluations" of the release (archived copies exist for December 2013, 2019, and 2025) document compliance with OMB data-quality and transparency standards.

**Confidentiality:** All published data are aggregate only. Individual respondent data are never published (with the partial exception of the commercial-bank interest-rate series). Pre-publication access is limited to responsible Board staff, with some material available to Board members and the FOMC as policy background.

## 3. History

- **1941–1942:** EO 8843 and Regulation W create the Board's consumer-credit mandate; the Board begins compiling and publishing consumer credit statistics. From 1942 to 1952 the Board actually published **three separate releases** (Consumer Instalment Credit of Industrial Banks; of Industrial Loan Companies; and Consumer Instalment Loans of the Principal Types of Financial Institutions), later consolidated.
- **Title evolution (per FRASER):** "Consumer Credit (G.19)," 1942–1976 → "Consumer Instalment Credit (G.19)," 1976–1996 → "Consumer Credit," 1996–present.
- **1955:** The Board begins the **quinquennial (every five years) Survey of Finance Companies (FR 3033s)**, which still provides benchmark data.
- **1972:** Terms-of-credit series added (Nixon wage-price program).
- **1983:** A major revision following an exhaustive review of the whole consumer-credit data program — focusing on items of highest policy priority and reducing reporting burden.
- **November 1986:** Release schedule accelerated from "about the middle" of the second month after the reference month to the fifth business day; the target has been met every month since.
- **1989:** Estimates of loans held in **pools of securitized assets** added (a series break).
- **1999:** Auto and "Other" categories combined into **"Nonrevolving"** because the split lacked a suitable benchmark; the report was reformatted to carry more history.
- **2003:** **Federal government and Sallie Mae (SLM Corp.) student loans** added; the line item was renamed simply "Federal government" in December 2009 after Sallie Mae's privatization was completed.
- **2006:** Another major methodology revision; flows and seasonal adjustment moved from level-based to flow-based, creating a break in the seasonally adjusted level at December 2006. Data for nonfinancial businesses and securitized pools are notably non-comparable across the January 2006 boundary.
- **2010:** FASB 166/167 accounting rules force most securitized assets back on balance sheet, shrinking off-book balances toward zero.
- **June 2012:** Commercial banks and savings institutions series combined into a single **"depository institutions"** sector (reflecting regulatory filing changes); flows added for all loan categories.
- **January/June 2020:** Off-book securitized balances reported only for depository institutions; the release shifted to reporting **aggregate "owned and managed" (on-book + off-book) receivables** for each sector.
- **July 2025:** The **nonfinancial business sector was retired** (its balances had greatly diminished and its source data were discontinued); retail credit formerly there is now captured in the finance company and other sectors. Simultaneously, the Board adopted **new credit union benchmark estimates** built on NCUA regulatory (call report) data, replacing the old survey-based benchmark — documented in FEDS Notes by Bruce, Chernousov, Hannon, and Scott (July 8, 2025).
- **Seasonal factors** are re-benchmarked annually before the September release using ten years of history.

This 80+ year run, with monthly observations back to 1943, makes the G.19 one of the longest continuously produced household-finance statistical series in the federal statistical system.

## 4. Methodology (Data Scientist's Perspective)

**Benchmark-and-indicator design.** Monthly estimates for each holder sector are interpolated between lower-frequency, comprehensive **benchmark** data using higher-frequency **indicator** series via proportional interpolation (an optimization minimizing period-to-period changes in the estimate-to-indicator ratio, constrained to hit each benchmark). Before the next benchmark arrives, monthly estimates are extrapolated from the last benchmark using indicator growth, then revised when the benchmark lands.

**Key source data:**

- **Depository institutions:** indicator from the voluntary weekly **FR 2644** (Weekly Report of Selected Assets and Liabilities of Domestically Chartered Commercial Banks), a stratified random panel of ~875 banks, linearly interpolated to month-end; benchmarks from regulatory Call Report data.
- **Finance companies:** indicator from the monthly **FR 2248** (Domestic Finance Company Report, currently ~50 reporting companies); benchmark from the **quinquennial Survey of Finance Companies (FR 3033s)** (most recent: ~2,400 companies surveyed, ~1,000 responding).
- **Credit unions:** since July 2025, benchmarked to NCUA call report data.
- **Federal government:** primarily Department of Education student loan data.
- **Nonprofit and educational institutions:** institutional data.

**Flows vs. levels.** Published flows are **break-adjusted** period-to-period changes in levels, designed to strip out methodological or source-data discontinuities (e.g., a loan portfolio moving in or out of scope). The growth rate on page 1 is flow ÷ prior level, which can differ from level-to-level growth in periods with breaks. Analysts should use flows, not first differences of levels, to compute growth rates.

**Seasonal adjustment** uses **X-12-ARIMA** applied to flows; factors are estimated annually and sum to zero within each calendar year; the seasonally adjusted level is built recursively from seasonally adjusted flows.

**Terms of credit** are quarterly: commercial-bank new-car and personal loan rates are simple unweighted averages of each bank's most common rate during the first calendar week of the middle month of each quarter; credit card plan rates come from a quarterly survey of card issuers; finance-company motor vehicle loan terms come from the FR 2248. Note the June 2024 FEDS Note ("A Note on Revolving Credit Estimates") addressing estimation issues around the pandemic-era swings.

**Known caveats for analysis:**
- Multiple documented series breaks (1989, 2003, 2006, 2010, 2012, 2020, 2025) — the Technical Q&A explicitly warns against comparing trends across the January 2006 boundary for some sectors.
- Data are national aggregates: no state, metro, or demographic breakdowns.
- Consumer credit *excluding* real-estate-secured debt — about one-third of household liabilities (mortgages, HELOCs) are out of scope; use the Z.1 Financial Accounts and/or the NY Fed's Household Debt and Credit Report for full household balance sheets.
- Terms-of-credit series are unweighted averages of "most common" quoted rates, not effective rates on actual loan volumes.

## 5. Access, Formats, and Distribution (Data Librarian's Perspective)

- **Official pages:** Current release, release dates, revisions announcements, historical data (HTML tables and PDF), charts, About/Technical Q&A at `federalreserve.gov/releases/g19/`.
- **Data Download Program (DDP):** Full machine-readable bulk download in CSV (and other formats), series identifiers like `G19/CCOUT/DTCOLHF_N.M`; coverage 1943–present (currently through roughly July 2026); also available as RSS/data feeds.
- **FRED (St. Louis Fed):** The entire release is ingested as FRED source release **"G.19 Consumer Credit"** (release ID 14), roughly 50 series covering SA levels/growth, NSA levels and flows by holder, and terms of credit — accessible via the FRED website, Excel add-in, and free API.
- **ALFRED (St. Louis Fed):** Vintage/real-time revision history for G.19 series, essential for replication of historical analyses.
- **FRASER (St. Louis Fed):** A full **digitized archival run** of the G.19 release (title ID 75), including PDF page images of releases back through the 1940s–1970s era (with issues browseable from 1976 forward in detail) plus archived Performance Evaluations (e.g., December 2013, 2019, 2025) and related historical documents such as Regulation W circulars.
- No registration, licensing, or fees anywhere; all channels are free and public. The Board publishes a standing release calendar on its Statistical Release Schedule.

## 6. Typical Users and Uses

- **The Federal Reserve itself (primary user):** Board and FOMC staff use the estimates as background for monetary policy decisions — monitoring household credit aggregates, the credit channel of policy, and (in its origins) administering credit controls.
- **Other government agencies:** OMB/CEA macroeconomic monitoring; Congress and GAO analyses of consumer debt; agencies tracking student lending (the federal government is itself a major measured sector).
- **Financial industry:** Bank and finance-company competitive analysts, credit-card issuers' market trackers, ratings agencies, and asset managers monitoring household leverage and terms of credit (auto-loan rates in particular are watched closely by auto ABS analysts).
- **Economists and academic researchers:** Long-run studies of household credit cycles, consumer spending behavior, financial stability, and credit market structure — the 1943 start date enables research spanning WWII, Korea, the postwar consumer-credit boom, the 2008 crisis, and the pandemic.
- **Journalists and think tanks:** The G.19 is the standard citation for monthly "credit card debt" and "car loan" news stories and for policy debates about household indebtedness.
- **Policy advocates:** Because the memo items isolate **student loans** and **motor vehicle loans**, the release is a go-to public dataset for advocacy and testimony on student-debt burdens and auto-loan affordability, and for monitoring the growth of federal vs. private student lending.

**Public benefits:** It is the **only official, free, comprehensive, national measure of non-mortgage household credit**, produced continuously for over 80 years with published methodology, revision history, and archival vintages. It enables evidence-based monetary policy, congressional oversight, consumer-finance journalism, and academic research that no private dataset (which charge licensing fees or cover narrower populations) can replicate — a point its OMB performance evaluations emphasize.

---

## 7. Preservation and Stewardship Notes

- The Board maintains permanent current and historical data tables and archives of each release; the St. Louis Fed's FRASER independently preserves digitized images of the entire release run (including the 1942–1952 three-release era and the "Consumer Instalment Credit" title years), and ALFRED preserves data vintages.
- Structural changes are documented in Announcements, Technical Q&As, and FEDS Notes (most recently July 2025), and the periodic Performance Evaluations serve as the release's formal self-documentation record under OMB statistical policy.
- Preservationists should note that off-book/on-book securitization splits and some retired sectors (commercial banks; savings institutions; nonfinancial businesses; pools of securitized assets) survive only in older releases and FRASER/ALFRED vintages — the current historical tables have been restructured around the current five sectors.

## Scope and methodology of this assessment

The G.19 is published by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System — an independent, **self-funded** agency whose budget is not set by congressional appropriations and whose staffing is outside the federal civil service. This structural fact shapes nearly every category below: the mechanisms that have endangered data at appropriated agencies (DOGE-directed cuts, appropriations riders, shutdowns) do not apply directly to the Fed. The relevant risks are instead (a) methodological changes made at the Board's own initiative, and (b) the broader 2025 political campaign against Fed independence.

One limitation: the USAJobs staffing tracker (usajobs-tracker.abigailhaddad.com) tracks USAJobs postings for executive-branch departments and agencies; the Federal Reserve hires through its own system and is not covered by that tracker (which itself was archived December 31, 2025). I therefore relied on press reporting and the Chair's own memo for staffing evidence.

## Category 1: Historical Data Availability

**Evidence — Gone/High Risk:** No evidence. All historical releases remain posted on federalreserve.gov; the full 1942-to-present run of releases is digitized on the St. Louis Fed's FRASER archive (title ID 75, including the "Consumer Instalment Credit" era); ALFRED preserves data vintages; the Data Download Program (DDP) carries levels back to January 1943. No wholesale removals found.

**Evidence — Moderate Risk:**
- The **nonfinancial business sector was retired from the release** beginning with the May 2025 release (published July 8, 2025). Board staff state that "our last data point is December 2019, and entries following this month will not be populated in the public repository" (FEDS Note, July 8, 2025). Post-2019 values for this sector had been held constant at $35 billion as placeholders after the Census Bureau discontinued the source data (Annual Retail Trade Survey consumer receivables item) in 2020 — so the removed post-2019 "data" were not real observations.
- Mitigations: data through 2019 remain available on the DDP; the change was announced April 7, 2025, in advance; a series break was added so flows and growth rates are unaffected; the rationale was documented in a public FEDS Note. The sector was ~0.7% of total consumer credit.
- Similar past precedent (2012 sector consolidations, 2020 on-book/off-book reporting change) also involved retiring data elements, all preserved in FRASER/ALFRED vintages.

**Verdict: Moderate Risk.** By the letter of the rubric, data elements that previously appeared in the dataset (the nonfinancial business sector line item) have been removed. However, the practical preservation risk is low: the removed elements were small, obsolete, and flat placeholders after 2019; all genuine historical data remain accessible on the Board's DDP and in three independent archival systems (FRASER, FRED, ALFRED). Users can still obtain accurate and reliable copies of everything the release ever meaningfully reported.

## Category 2: Future Data Availability

**Evidence — No Known Issue:**
- The release has been published **on schedule every month** throughout 2025 and into 2026 (e.g., May 7, July 8, September 8, October 7, November 7, December 5, 2025 releases all posted on their scheduled dates), continuing the "fifth business day" target met continuously since 1986. A standing release calendar is maintained.
- The **source-survey ICRs are active and repeatedly renewed**: FR 2248 (Domestic Finance Company Report, OMB No. 7100-0005) was extended with approvals on 2025-03-31, 2025-09-08, and 2026-03-31, expiring 05/31/2027, with a revision proposal published July 9, 2026 (91 FR, effective June 2027); the Survey of Finance Companies (FR 3033p/s, OMB No. 7100-0277) was extended for three years with revision on April 30, 2025 (90 FR, 2025-07410).
- When the CUNA credit-union indicator survey was discontinued, the Board **replaced it** (America's Credit Unions estimates derived from Equifax tradeline data) rather than dropping the series — publication continuity was preserved.
- The Fed is self-funded; no appropriations lapse or shutdown can halt the release.

**Verdict: No Known Issue.** Publication has continued on time, clearances are current, and source-data losses have been actively backfilled rather than allowed to break the series.

**Evidence — High Risk (considered and rejected):** The February 2025 executive order on presidential supervision of independent agencies (with a monetary-policy carve-out) and the sustained campaign against Fed independence (Cook removal attempt, Powell threats, Miran's "shibboleth" dismissal of independence) represent genuine institutional pressure. But nothing in the record connects any of this to the G.19 or to the Fed's statistical program: no presidential action touches the G.19's ICRs, no negative policy note appears on the release site, and the G.19 contains none of the content types (climate, DEI, environmental justice) targeted for removal across the administration. Press and archival surveys of the 2025 data-removal wave (Brookings, National Security Archive, Nikkei, Wikipedia's removals tracker) document extensive removals at EPA, NASA, NOAA, CDC, CEQ, USGCRP, and data.gov — **none at the Federal Reserve Board's statistical releases**.

**Evidence — Moderate Risk (considered):** The 2025 changes to the release (sector retirement, benchmark update, indicator replacement, and the December 2025 DDP/FRED interface change) are "significant changes" — but they were driven by source-data discontinuation (Census survey ended 2020), market-structure change, and technical modernization, not administration priorities, and each was announced in advance and documented publicly. The Board's alignment with the government-wide efficiency push (Powell's staffing memo) is arguably "in accordance with Administration priorities," but it does not affect what data the G.19 collects or publishes.

**Verdict: No Known Issue.** Since January 2025 there are no administration-driven changes to what the G.19 collects and publishes. The caveat worth recording for a preservationist: the larger assault on Fed independence is a systemic tail risk — an institution whose leadership is captured could eventually compromise its statistical output — but nothing observed to date indicates any intent or mechanism directed at this dataset.

## Summary of Risk Levels

**Historical Data Availability: Moderate Risk**
(One sector's line item removed post-2019 with announced rationale; all meaningful historical data remain fully accessible via DDP, FRASER, FRED, and ALFRED.)

**Future Data Availability: No Known Issue**
(Monthly publication on schedule throughout 2025–26; all source-survey ICRs active and renewed; discontinued source data actively replaced.)

**Data Quality: Moderate Risk**
(Frequency and timeliness maintained and credit-union coverage improved, but sector granularity was reduced, the download interface is in transition, and the 10% staff drawdown is an emerging resource risk.)

**Statutory Context: No Known Issue**
(Federal Reserve Act authority explicitly cited in collection instruments; required for monetary-policy implementation; only partial private substitutes exist; monetary policy expressly carved out of the 2025 executive-order supervision regime.)

**Staffing and Funding: Moderate Risk**
(Planned ~10% voluntary/attrition-based workforce reduction over several years; threatened leadership change — Cook removal attempt litigated, Powell's chair term ending May 2026 with an openly political succession — but no budget cuts and no removals consummated.)

**Policy: No Known Issue**
(All 2025 changes were technical, pre-announced, and documented, not administration-driven; the Fed's statistical releases are absent from every documented account of the administration's data-removal campaign.)

**Overall assessment:** The G.19 sits at low-to-moderate preservation risk. The principal documented harms are self-inflicted, well-documented methodological housekeeping (a defunct sector retired, sources swapped), fully mitigated by the dataset's exceptional archival redundancy (Board DDP, FRASER, FRED, ALFRED). The largest genuine threat is not to this dataset specifically but to the institution: the ongoing campaign against Federal Reserve independence and the 2026 leadership transition, which constitutes a systemic — though currently speculative — risk to the continued nonpolitical production of all Fed statistics.
